# Academic Standing / Suspension Appeal

## When this applies
If your ASU GPA falls below a 2.0, you're placed on **academic warning**, then **probation**, then **suspension** if it doesn't improve — the exact thresholds and terms are on your DARS report's GPA block. Suspension means you cannot register for the next term unless the suspension is successfully appealed or served.

## Steps to appeal
1. Log in to [My ASU](https://my.asu.edu) → **Academic Standing** → **Appeal Suspension** (only visible once you're actually suspended — it won't show for warning/probation).
2. Write the appeal statement: what caused the drop (be specific and honest — documented circumstances like illness, family emergency, or unexpected work hours carry more weight than a general "I struggled"), and a concrete plan for the next term (reduced course load, tutoring, specific support resources).
3. Attach supporting documentation if you have it (medical note, counselor letter, etc.) — not required, but strengthens the appeal.
4. Submit before the stated deadline for the upcoming term; late appeals are rarely reviewed in time to register.

## What actually gets appeals approved
Appeals committees are looking for a plan, not just an explanation. "I'll try harder" gets denied more often than "I'm enrolling in 12 credits instead of 18, meeting with a tutor weekly for MAT 265, and using the counseling center's biweekly check-in." If you don't have a concrete plan yet, that's exactly what an advising appointment is for — book one before writing the appeal, not after.

## If the appeal is denied
You can typically sit out a term (suspension is usually one semester) and petition to return, or transfer credits from a community college during the suspension term to keep progress moving — talk to an advisor about which path protects your financial aid and catalog year.

# Add/Drop a Class

## Deadlines
The add/drop period runs through the first week of a full-length session (shorter for 7.5-week sessions — check the [Academic Calendar](https://students.asu.edu/academic-calendar)). Drops within this window leave no record on the transcript and are fully refunded; after it ends, a drop becomes a withdrawal (see the withdrawal entry) instead.

## Steps to add a class
1. On [My ASU](https://my.asu.edu), go to **My Classes** → **Add a Class**.
2. Search by course number or subject, and check the section has open seats and no unmet prerequisite or corequisite hold.
3. If a class is full, you can join the **waitlist** — you'll be auto-enrolled if a seat opens, as long as you have no schedule conflict at that time.
4. Review the updated schedule for time conflicts before confirming.

## Steps to drop a class
1. **My Classes** → select the class → **Drop**.
2. Confirm. If you're within the add/drop window, no W appears and tuition for that class is refunded.

## What people usually get stuck on
- A **prerequisite hold** on a course you've actually completed (e.g. transfer credit not yet posted) requires an advisor override — bring an unofficial transcript or AP/IB score report to the appointment, it goes faster.
- Waitlist auto-enrollment silently fails if it would drop you below full-time or create a time conflict — check your email confirmation, don't assume you're in.
- Dropping your **last class** in a term is a full withdrawal from the term, not a drop, and has separate financial aid and enrollment-verification consequences — talk to an advisor first.

# Change of Major

## When you can do it yourself
If the major you want is **open enrollment** (not competitive/capacity-limited), you can change it directly:
1. Log in to [My ASU](https://my.asu.edu) → **My Programs** → **Request a Change of Major**.
2. Select the new major/college and submit. It usually processes within a few business days and does not require an appointment.

## When it needs an advisor
Some majors (e.g. many Engineering, Nursing, Business majors) are **restricted** — they require minimum GPA, specific prerequisite courses completed, or a formal application. For these:
1. Check the major's admission requirement page on the [ASU Degree Search](https://degrees.apps.asu.edu) — look for "change of major requirements," not just the general catalog description.
2. If you meet the stated requirements, the change-of-major request in My ASU will usually still go through, but restricted majors can flag for manual review.
3. If you don't yet meet the requirements (e.g. still finishing a required prerequisite), the request will be denied and you'll need to work with an advisor on a plan to become eligible.

## Before you request the change
Run the DARS "what-if" audit for the target major first (My ASU → **My Program** → **What-If Analysis**) — it shows how your completed courses would apply under the new major, which is usually the actual question behind "should I switch."

## The advisory case
If the real question is *"is this even the right major for me,"* that's not a form — it's worth talking to an advisor with your DARS what-if in hand. A bot can tell you what would transfer; it shouldn't be the one telling you whether to switch.

# Course Withdrawal

## Deadlines
A course withdrawal must be submitted by the deadline posted on the [ASU Academic Calendar](https://students.asu.edu/academic-calendar) for that term — typically the Friday of the 12th week of a full-length fall/spring session (earlier for 7.5-week sessions). After that date, withdrawal requires a petition and is not guaranteed.

## Steps
1. Log in to [My ASU](https://my.asu.edu) and go to **My Classes**.
2. Select the course you want to withdraw from and choose **Withdraw**.
3. Confirm the withdrawal — this replaces your grade with a **W**, which does not count toward GPA but does count toward attempted credit hours.
4. If you're on financial aid, check with Financial Aid before confirming: dropping below full-time status can affect eligibility.
5. Withdrawal is final for that term once confirmed; you cannot re-add the course after this point.

## The four things people get wrong
- Withdrawing does **not** refund tuition after the add/drop period — refund percentage is tied to the deadline you withdraw by, not the withdrawal itself.
- A W still shows on the transcript and counts toward the **maximum-attempts** limit for repeated courses.
- International students on an F-1/J-1 visa should confirm minimum full-time enrollment with ISSC before withdrawing — this can affect visa status.
- If the course is a prerequisite for something already registered next term, withdrawing can silently drop you from the downstream course — check your schedule after withdrawing.

You do not need an advising appointment to withdraw. You do need one if you're unsure how the W affects a specific degree requirement or your financial aid — that's where this stops being a form question.

# Late Add / Late Drop Petition

## When you need this
The add/drop window has closed and either: (a) you need to add a class you were mistakenly left out of (instructor permission, registration error), or (b) you need to drop a class without it becoming a W and without waiting for the withdrawal deadline.

## Steps
1. Get instructor and department approval first — most petitions are denied without it. Email the instructor explaining the situation and ask them to confirm approval in writing (a reply-all email is enough).
2. Submit the **Petition for Late Registration Changes** through your college's student services office — this is a form, not a My ASU self-service flow; each college hosts its own version, search "[your college] late registration petition."
3. Attach the instructor approval and a brief explanation of why the request is late (registration hold that was resolved late, advising error, documented emergency, etc. — "I forgot" is rarely approved).
4. Processing typically takes 1–2 weeks. You remain responsible for coursework/attendance in the class while the petition is pending if you're trying to add.

## What trips people up
- Petitions filed for reasons within the student's control (didn't check My ASU, missed the deadline knowingly) are usually denied — the petition exists for registration errors and documented emergencies, not for changing your mind late.
- This is different from a course withdrawal: a withdrawal is always available up to its own deadline and doesn't need a petition. Only use this form if you're trying to act *after* both the add/drop and withdrawal windows, or need a drop with no W recorded.

# Requesting a Transcript

## Official transcript
1. Go to [My ASU](https://my.asu.edu) → **My Academics** → **Order Official Transcript** (this hands off to the National Student Clearinghouse).
2. Choose electronic (PDF, usually available within minutes once processed) or paper (mailed, takes longer).
3. There's a small per-copy fee. A **hold on your account** (financial, judicial, or advising) blocks transcript release — the order page will say so; clearing the hold is a separate step from placing the order.

## Unofficial transcript
Available free, instantly, in My ASU → **My Academics** → **View Unofficial Transcript**. Use this for your own planning — it's not accepted for most external submissions, which require the official version.

## Common snag
Grad school and employer portals often want the transcript sent **directly** from ASU, not uploaded by you. When ordering, choose the electronic delivery option and enter the receiving institution's email or portal address exactly as they specify — a transcript emailed to yourself instead of the institution gets rejected by most application systems.

title: 4+1 Accelerated Master's Programs
raw_content:
Why choose an accelerated master’s program?
The accelerated master’s program offers highly committed undergraduate students the option to combine undergraduate degree requirements with graduate coursework, resulting in faster degree completion.
- Pay less for overall graduate coursework by taking graduate-level courses at the undergraduate tuition price
- Earn more money upon graduation: on average, starting salaries for people holding master’s degrees are 31% higher than those with only a bachelor’s degree
- Cover a portion of your master’s degree with your undergraduate scholarship; some limitations may apply
- Reduce the total amount of student loans needed for a master’s degree
- Earn a master’s degree in one year instead of the typical two (for some programs)
- Complete both programs faster than your peers
- Get started on your career faster
- Less coursework means less time and money spent
- Advance in your career faster than your peers
- Signal to future employers you’re a highly competitive candidate
- Accelerate your placement into a potential PhD program
- Enter the workforce with advanced knowledge and skills
- Employment in jobs requiring a master's degree is expected to grow by 17% from 2016-2026

Online Undergraduate Research Scholars (OURS) program
The College of Liberal Arts and Sciences and EdPlus have developed the Online Undergraduate Research Scholars (OURS) program to address the pressing challenge of offering quality research opportunities to ASU Online students at scale.
The OURS program offers research experiences across a wide range of disciplines including natural sciences, social sciences and humanities. These types of experiential learning opportunities differentiate ASU from other institutions that offer online degree programs.
